before: They lit an altar for a drink offering to the demons, brought the martyr and stood him beside it, and ordered him to stretch his right hand out over the altar with the palm turned upward. They used the hand as a bronze altar, wickedly placing burning incense in it. For they hoped that the hand would be wrestled down by the force of the fire and would quickly be compelled to drop the incense onto the altar. What a tangled trick of the impious! “Since,” they say, “we have not bent his resolve with countless wounds, let us at least bend the hand of this stubborn wrestler in the fire. Since we have not shaken his soul with various devices, let us at least bring his right hand to the fire and make it waver.” But the wretches did not profit even from this hope. The fire gnawed through the hand, but the hand remained, bearing the flame as though it were ash. It did not turn its back to the attacking fire like a deserter, but stood unshaken, proving itself best against the fire, and giving the martyr the words of the Prophet to speak: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Psalm 18:34; Psalm 17:35 LXX). Fire grappled with a hand, and the fire was found to bear the marks of defeat. A wrestling match was joined between the fire and the martyr’s right hand, but the victory of the right hand’s wrestling moves was something new: the fire fell through the middle of the hand, while the hand remained stretched out for the contest. O hand more stubborn than fire! O hand that never learned to bend to fire! O fire that was taught to be defeated by a hand! Iron yields to the tyranny of fire and is softened. Bronze gives way to the power of fire. Even the resistance of stones, as we know, is overcome by it. But the force of fire that overpowers everything did not bend the martyr’s stretched-out right hand, even as it burned it. Fittingly the martyr might cry out to the Master: “You held my right hand, and in your counsel you guided me, and with glory you received me” (Psalm 73:24; Psalm 72:24 LXX). What shall I call you, noble soldier of Christ? Shall I call you a statue? I fall far short of your endurance. For fire, receiving it, softens a statue, but it could not make your right hand appear to move. If I call you iron, I find that even this image falls short of your courage. For you alone persuaded the fire not to force a hand. You alone made your right hand an altar. You alone with a burning right hand struck the faces of the demons, and then with a charred hand you melted their heads along with it; now with that hand burned to ashes you blind their armies as you trample them. But why do I diminish the champion with childish stammering? Let us yield the hymn in his honor to more magnificent tongues. Let us summon the louder trumpets of the teachers for him. Rise up now for me, brilliant painters of athletic achievements. Magnify with your arts the mutilated image of the commander. Illuminate with the colors of your wisdom the crowned victor whom I have painted too dimly. May I depart defeated by your painting of the martyr’s feats. I rejoice today to be defeated by such a victory of your strength. Let me see the wrestling match of the hand against the fire painted by you more accurately. Let me see the wrestler drawn more brightly on your image. Let the demons weep, struck now too by the martyr’s feats in your work. Let the burning hand be shown again to them, victorious. Let Christ also, the umpire of the wrestling matches, be inscribed on the tablet—to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
